After the Pandavas leave for the forest, Dhritarashtra is uneasy, and seeks Vidura’s advice, said Kidambi Narayanan in a discourse. He says Vidura knows dharma sukshma. Dharma sukshma goes beyond merely knowing the rules. It means a person knows how to react in a particular situation, how to analyse a situation and come to the right conclusion. Only those with experience in dealing with problems of various kinds will have dharma sukshma. Dhritarashtra is aware that Vidura has jnana, which includes knowledge of dharma too. Dhritarashtra is worried. He knows his family cannot get away unhurt if they hurt the Pandavas. Not only will they have to face the wrath of the Pandavas, but will have to deal with the displeasure of the people too. He tells Vidura that whatever Sakuni did was for the welfare of Duryodhana. But he knows that dharma was not adhered to in his court. He asks Vidura how to atone for what happened in the royal assembly.

Vidura says seeking wealth and pleasures must be within the boundaries of dharma. The foundation of governance is dharma. Dhritarashtra must not only be keen to protect his sons, but must also want to protect the Pandavas. “You are prejudiced against the Pandavas. You must come out of this mindset. A king should not covet other people’s wealth. At least from now on, stop troubling the Pandavas. If the Kauravas continue to torment the Pandavas, your family will be destroyed. The Pandavas should be brought back. Yudhishthira is not ambitious. A kingdom will be safe only in the hands of such a king,” Vidura tells Dhritarashtra. Vidura’s words about Yudhishthira remind us of Rama’s attitude to kingship. Rama was unaffected by the possibility of being king, or about His exile. That is the hallmark of a good leader.
